title: Handle lead-acid batteries safely
summary: Move, connect, charge and store lead-acid batteries without acid burns, short-circuit burns, hydrogen explosions or back injuries. Covers car, golf cart, forklift, floor scrubber, UPS and solar batteries.

materials.item: Distilled or deionized water for topping up flooded batteries (Trojan allows only these and warns water picks up impurities from containers; clean rainwater caught straight into a clean plastic container is an unapproved last resort)
Cloth or non-metal brush for cleaning terminals

steps.text: Put on glasses and gloves. Check the battery before you touch it: cracks, bulges, leaks, white crust, a wet top.
steps.warn: A cracked or bulging battery can pour acid when tipped. Keep it upright.

steps.text: Wrap the handle of your wrench in tape, leaving only the jaws bare.
steps.warn: A wrench across the terminals of a big battery can weld itself on, glow red and burst the battery.

steps.text: On a vehicle or machine, switch everything off. Undo the negative (−, black) lead first, then the positive (+, red). When reconnecting, positive first and negative last.
steps.warn: If you undo the positive while the negative is still on, a wrench touching the frame makes a dead short.

steps.text: Lift with both hands by the handles or a strap, knees bent, battery close to your body. Car batteries can weigh 14–27 kg (30–60 lb) or more (CCOHS garages), and a T-105 golf cart battery 28 kg (62 lb) (Trojan T-105). Forklift and other industrial batteries can weigh 900 kg (2,000 lb) or more and need machinery (CCOHS charging).
steps.warn: Don't hug a battery to your chest or let it tilt. Acid can slop out of the vents.

steps.text: Carry it upright, strapped down, with the terminals covered by a cap, a rag or tape, away from metal tools.

Charge in a ventilated place, away from sparks and flames (Trojan guide, CCOHS garages), and not in a bedroom. Connect the charger to the battery before switching the charger on. Switch off before unclipping (CCOHS garages).
steps.warn: Charging makes hydrogen. A spark at the terminals can blow the top off the battery.

steps.text: On flooded batteries with removable caps, top up after a full charge, to the fill mark, with distilled or deionized water: Trojan says impurities in tap water damage the battery. Only if the plates show before charging, add just enough to cover them first. Never add acid (Trojan guide).
steps.warn: Don't overfill. Acid will bubble out during the next charge.

steps.text: Clean crust off terminals with baking soda in water (Trojan mixes about 60 ml in a litre) and a cloth or non-metal brush, then rinse with clean water. Keep it out of the cells (Trojan guide).

Store batteries fully charged in a cool, dry place. Check a flooded one every 4–6 weeks and recharge it when it falls to about 70% (12.4 V); check sealed AGM and gel ones every 2–3 months and recharge at 75% (Trojan guide).
steps.warn: A flat battery can freeze and crack a few degrees below zero. A fully charged one survives hard frost (Trojan guide).

steps.text: Neutralise any spill with baking soda until it stops fizzing (Trojan guide, CCOHS garages), soak it up with dirt or sawdust, and rinse. Keep dead batteries upright on a tray outdoors, away from water sources.

notes:
## What's inside

A 12 V lead-acid battery is six cells of about 2.1 V each, so about 12.7 V when full; sealed AGM and gel types read a little higher (Trojan guide). Lead plates sit in dilute sulphuric acid.

| Type | How to tell | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Flooded (wet) | Removable caps on top | Can be topped up with distilled water. Must stay upright |
| AGM | Sealed, often marked AGM | Acid held in glass mat. Don't open, never add water, never equalise (Trojan guide). Tolerates tipping better |
| Gel | Sealed, marked gel | Use the charger's gel setting. Don't open, never add water, never equalise (Trojan guide) |

Trojan's deep-cycle batteries charge at about 14.7 V (flooded) or 14.4 V (AGM and gel) and float at 13.5 V, at 25 °C (Trojan guide). Other makers differ a little, so check the label if there is one.

## Short circuits

A car battery can push hundreds of amps through a short. That is enough to melt a wrench, a ring or a watch strap in seconds. A ring shorted across a terminal can burn a finger to the bone. Take jewellery off and use insulated tools (Trojan guide). Keep tools and other metal off the battery top (CCOHS garages).

## Hydrogen

Hydrogen burns or explodes when it makes up between about 4% and 72% of the air (CCOHS charging). It collects in the cells and under the lid during and just after charging. That is why the last jump-start clamp goes on bare engine metal at least 30 cm (12 in) from the battery, not on the battery's negative post (CCOHS garages).

## Freezing

| State of charge | Roughly freezes at |
|---|---|
| Full | well below −40 °C |
| Half | about −20 °C |
| Flat | not far below 0 °C, about −10 °C or warmer |

These follow Trojan's freezing-point table by specific gravity (Trojan guide). Never charge or jump-start a frozen battery (Trojan guide, CCOHS garages). Let it thaw first, and check for cracks.

## Common mistakes

- Charging a frozen or bulging battery.
- Topping up with tap water or salty water instead of distilled water.
- Leaving a battery flat after use. It sulphates and loses capacity fast; Trojan says to charge fully after each use (Trojan guide).
- Wearing a ring or watch while working on terminals.
- Mixing old and new batteries in one bank: the new ones can be overcharged and the old ones undercharged (Trojan maintenance, on flooded banks).
